newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope to preach harmony on April Sarajevo trip.
newsitem.headline: Pope to preach harmony on April Sarajevo trip.

text.p: Pope John Paul announced on Thursday he would visit Bosnia in April to preach religious reconciliation to a land torn apart by four years of inter-communal war underscored by religious divisions.

A Vatican statement said the head of the Roman Catholic church would go to Sarajevo on April 13, for a trip postponed from September 1994 when separatist Serb forces laying siege to the Bosnian capital said they could not guarantee his safety.
The Pope will seek "to promote understanding and cooperation with the members of all religious confessions" during his one-day visit, the statement said.

Religion underlies the conflict which has torn apart Bosnia, a united region under former Yugoslavia, now largely divided into separate communities of Orthodox Serbs, Roman Catholic Croats and Moslems -- all of them ethnic Slavs.
The statement said the Pope hoped his visit would help "efforts being made to build a just peace and to restore a full and harmonious civil life in that country".

It added that the Pope was making the visit "above all to encourage the Catholic community in Bosnia-Herzegovina to carry on its active Christian witness in every part of the country" and to preach cooperation among religions.
The Pope has spoken often of the four-year Yugoslav conflict and Sarajevo's siege, describing the city as a symbol of human suffering.

The visit, which the Vatican says fulfils "a long-cherished desire" held by the Pope, will be the 76-year-old Pontiff's first overseas trip of 1997 and his first since having his appendix removed late last year.

Church officials in Sarajevo, anticipating the Vatican's confirmation of the Pope's visit, have said the Pontiff will meet local Roman Catholic clergy, Bosnian government leaders and will celebrate mass.
Bosnia's three-man collective presidency, comprising Moslem, Croat and Serb members, had issued an invitation to the Pope in November to go to Sarajevo.
The Pope visited overwhelmingly Catholic Croatia in 1994, drawing huge crowds in the capital Zagreb. He travelled to Slovenia, another former Yugoslav republic, last year.

The Sarajevo trip begins a busy travel schedule for the Pope for the rest of the year. The Vatican has confirmed trips to Prague, Poland, Paris and Brazil and the Pope is expected to make a brief visit to Lebanon this spring.
Doctors who performed the appendectomy had urged the Pope, the most travelled in history, to slow down.
